en: The *Prakaraṇapañcikā*, composed by the Great Professor Śālikanātha Miśra, who bore the burden of the tradition of the venerable teacher Prabhākara.
The work titled *Mīmāṃsājīvarakṣā*, adorned with the commentary named *Nyāyasiddhi* and the gloss on difficult passages (*viṣamasthala-ṭippaṇī*).
The Tenth Chapter.

Having thoroughly reflected upon the intention of the teacher Prabhākara, this *Mīmāṃsājīvarakṣā* (Protection of the Life of Mīmāṃsā), which is the refutation of momentariness, is now set forth. // 1 //
In this regard, those who follow the doctrine of the Sugata assert that all entities indeed perish moment by moment.
But what is their means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for this?
First of all, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is not capable of perceiving momentariness.
For one who examines the state of a pillar and so forth with extreme precision, there is an absence of the determination of momentariness.
One might think: "Momentariness is not something external to the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of an entity;
therefore, through the very experience of the entity, perception directly realizes momentariness as well."
The wise consider this to be a mere wishful thought;
for indeed, the principle that "the determination of objects is grounded in consciousness" is an undisputed tenet among all theorists.
Therefore, this momentariness of an entity, being its very nature, is established as non-different from consciousness when it enters into consciousness, and not otherwise.
And since he did not observe consciousness arising in that manner,
how could it be included within the intrinsic nature of an entity?
And how much less could there be an awakening through the awakening to that [consciousness]?
Now, they might think: "Although momentariness is being perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it has not entered the path of certain determination; therefore, it appears as if ungrasped.
Nevertheless, direct perception is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding it.
For in those cases where the operation of direct perception—which is by nature free from conceptual construction—is followed by a subsequent conceptual cognition (*savikalpakapratyaya*),"

Regarding this, the followers of the Sugata (Buddhists) maintain that direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the [only] valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). However, for those whose minds are shrouded by the darkness of their own tenets, the claim that "that which does not give rise to the cognition 'this is perceived' is not apprehended through direct perception" is a mere flourish of empty words.
As for what some have said— that perception is momentary and, by having as its object a thing delimited by its own time, makes known that [thing's] momentariness—
that too is the talk of a child.
Momentariness indeed consists in existing for only a single moment.
Perception does not apprehend that "this very thing exists at this very time," because perception maintains indifference toward other times.
On the contrary, perception characterized by recognition (pratyabhijñā) actually casts momentariness far away,
because it conceives of an entity as persisting through preceding and succeeding times.
Furthermore, inference— which is dependent upon the apprehension of a relationship— is not able to take momentariness as its subject (pakṣa).
Because there is an absence of cognition of a relationship with any [other] sign (*liṅga*) in connection with that [object].
Indeed, a cognition of a relationship does not arise when the relata are not perceived.
Furthermore, those who follow the doctrine of the Sugata do not accept a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that is distinct from these two.
The Buddhists mock this [position] as being like "confusing the sky.
For they proclaim that momentariness is to be understood through inference based on essential identity (*svabhāvahetu*).
But what, then, is that inference?
Whatever exists is momentary,
and all things exist; thus, when the probandum is invariably concomitant with existence alone, this constitutes a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*),
just as the property of being a *śiṃśapā* tree is [the reason] for being a tree.
For "treeness" is invariably concomitant with being a *śiṃśapā* tree;
likewise here too, momentariness is invariably concomitant with existence alone.
But how is this invariable concomitance with that [existence] alone established?
Because a subverting proof operates against the contrary position;
for if there were non-momentariness, the non-perception of the pervader would subvert existence.
For existence is indeed the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritā*).
There is no other [alternative] whatsoever;
and that [activity] is pervaded by succession and simultaneity, because these two are mutually exclusive, such that the negation of one is necessarily concomitant with the affirmation of the other.
Furthermore, neither succession nor simultaneity is possible in non-momentary entities; yet,
when these two [succession and simultaneity] are excluded, they also exclude existence itself, just as the exclusion of "treeness" excludes "śiṃśapā-ness."
How is it that non-momentary things lack causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) through either succession or simultaneity?
On this point, they say: Is a non-momentary entity by its very nature the producer of causal efficiency, or is it not of that nature?
There is no other alternative. In that regard, if the former position were accepted, all purposeful activities would be completed in a single moment alone;
and since it is impossible to perform again what has already been performed, [the latter position must be accepted].

Because it would be devoid of the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-sāmarthya*) in the subsequent moment, it would follow that it possesses the characteristic of non-existence, resulting in the loss of its non-momentary nature.
However, if one relies on the second alternative, then no causal efficiency would ever be produced from it at any time.
It would result in the very consequence that [the entity] lacks the characteristic of existence.

It might be thought: "Even though an entity is capable by its own nature, it produces an effect only at certain times due to the presence of auxiliary causes, and not at other times due to their absence."
Even that [auxiliary] cannot withstand scrutiny:
does it indeed initiate something together with [the primary cause], or not?
For even if it were to initiate [something], it would have to be of the same nature as the entity intended to be the means for accomplishing a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
Furthermore, one must consider the alternative: "or is it something that does not constitute its own nature"?
In the case of the position that there is no production, the meaning of "dependence" must be stated;
for indeed, dependence upon something that provides no assistance is not meaningful.

Furthermore, if there were the commencement of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity that is intended to be the means for accomplishing a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), it would follow that the entity itself must also arise.
For that which is not arising cannot possess an arising intrinsic nature,
because the superimposition of contradictory properties necessarily entails difference.
Furthermore, if one accepts the arising of a new state [of the entity], the position that things are non-momentary (akṣaṇika) is utterly destroyed.
For if one admits the commencement of something that does not constitute the very nature of the entity, that entity would be incapable of producing an effect prior to that commencement;
thus, causal efficiency (arthakriyā) cannot be established through a sequence from a non-momentary thing.
Therefore, causal efficiency must arise from something external that comes from elsewhere,
because it exists when that [external thing] is present and does not exist when it is absent.
And there is no other mode besides these two—exclusion and non-exclusion—because one does not perceive the coexistence of two mutually contradictory things in a single locus.
Now, even a momentary entity possesses a nature capable of producing its own action and effect; [is it not so?]
Or [if it is] "not having that as its intrinsic nature," this does not transcend the aforementioned conceptual alternatives (kalpanā).
In that case, there could be no dependence upon auxiliary causes for that which has an intrinsic nature capable of producing causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
For no purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) arises from that which lacks capacity.
Listen to the supreme secret of the Sugatas: an entity (*bhāva*), having reached its final moment, possesses a nature capable of producing purposeful activity and initiates only a single effect.
Why, then, does it not produce [that effect] even without its auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*)?
If that which is independent is the producer, what kind of auxiliary function could it possibly have? Thus, being independent, it does not act as a producer.
If that which is independent is the producer, [it cannot have auxiliaries].

It must also be stated what kind of "cooperation" (sahakāritā) it possesses. To this we reply: as for the statement that was made—"Why does it not act even without its auxiliaries?"—that is merely a manifestation of a lack of skill regarding the Sugata’s doctrine.
For a momentary entity does not exist without its auxiliary causes; how can that which is non-existent produce an effect?
And that which does exist is not "that" [the same thing].
Nothing has been diminished.
To the objection, "Why is it that [the effect] does not arise even when devoid of its auxiliary causes?
the answer must be stated in terms of the nature of the causes: they simply do not exist in such a way [to produce it].
And they "cultivate" [the effect] as well;
that is, the state of performing a single action is the cooperation (*sahakāritā*) of those existing at the final moment.
But surely, since even they are producers independent of anything else, why do they not initiate another effect?
In this matter as well, we are powerless; we are only able to grant our consent that "whatever entities begin, let them begin.
And these very producers, though they exist, produce only that [which is already determined].
Our admission is limited only to what we ourselves perceive.
But one might ask: "If it has been accomplished by one, what does the other do?"
This might be so in the case of successive causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), but in the case of simultaneous action (*sahakriyā*), there is simply no such thing as "it has been done.
[Objection: But surely, even from a single cause, that [result] is established?
What else do they do?
It is not so;
they are not acting with prior reflection.
By which they might reflect thus:
"Another person, even without us, is capable of doing this; we have no power here."
But since their presence is dependent upon causes, they cannot help but exist; so what is the inconsistency?
[Objection: But how can a single effect arise from multiple [causes]?
For it is indeed the difference in causes that is the cause for the difference in the effect.
Otherwise, it would follow that [the effect] occurs at all times.
It is replied: the difference in the effect does not arise from a difference in the auxiliary causes (sahakārikāraṇa), but rather from a difference in the causal totality (sāmagrī).

For those who have exerted effort in the *Hetubindu*, this [point] is easily understood without strain. Therefore, even regarding momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), there is no room for an objection similar to that directed against the position of non-momentariness.
For, through the transformation of a succession of moments, such a moment as [the one capable of producing an effect] arises from seeds and the like.
Since the sprout appears immediately after [the seed] has arisen without depending on any other cause, one might object:
"Even so, how can the recognition ‘this is that very same thing’ be established regarding the successive moments of the seed and so forth?
Furthermore, it should not be argued: "How can inference establish itself when it contradicts the perception of recognition?"
Alternatively, there would be the undesirable consequence of inferring coldness even in fire upon its acquisition of self-nature.

The resolution is stated as follows: regarding those moments, for one who is unable to reflect upon their absolute difference—despite it being perceived through extreme similarity—the conventional usage of non-difference proceeds, based on the apprehension of difference.
It is like the conventional usage of "silver" with respect to mother-of-pearl;
nor is there any contradiction with the arising of inference,
because the fulfillment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) would otherwise be inexplicable.
Recognition, however, is established even through the non-apprehension of difference; thus, it is faultless.
For this very reason, the elders say: "Inference is indeed stronger than even perception.
And we see that this alone is logical.
The sense faculty operates upon what is present;

it does not, however, touch that which possesses the nature of having been connected at a prior time, nor does the mental impression (bhāvanā) produced by a previous experience reach out to this "thisness" (idantā) which consists in connection with another time.
This has been explained by the recognition of a flame;
moreover, the inevitable destruction of produced entities is perceived,
and from this as well, their momentary perishability can be inferred.
For instance: if something is certain to occur for these [entities], there is no dependence upon other causes for it;
and the destruction of produced things is certain to occur.
An inference based on the perception of a mark characterized by the pervasion of the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*) refutes the dependence of destruction upon another cause.

For the state of being necessarily occurring (*dhruvabhāvitā*) is perceived as being pervaded by independence, which is the opposite of the dependence on another cause that is being negated; this [independence] establishes the non-dependence of destruction upon another cause, and thereby excludes its opposite, namely, dependence on another cause.
For those things which depend upon other causes do not necessarily occur;
as, for example, the dyeing of a cloth and so forth.
Therefore, the perception of that which is pervaded by necessary occurrence— characterized by independence from other causes and being contrary to the state of being dependent on other causes—
is itself the non-perception of non-necessary occurrence. From this non-perception of non-necessary occurrence, [the necessary occurrence is established].
There is no dependence on another cause for destruction;
likewise, if entities were also to depend upon another cause for their destruction apart from their own causes,
then there would be no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish a rule regarding the presence of that other cause.
Even if something were produced, it would not fail to perish;
since its destruction follows immediately upon its arising from its own cause, the momentary nature of all things is established.
Furthermore, this must be considered:
when produced things arise from their own causes, are they born with a perishable nature,
or with a non-perishable nature?
Those whose nature is perishable dissolve immediately after their arising and are thus subject to momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgin*).
However, those whose nature is imperishable could never perish.
Furthermore, their destruction cannot be brought about by another cause.
Because it cannot withstand analysis: for that destruction which arises, is it non-different from the entity,
or is it different?
It is not, first of all, non-different,
because of the difference in causes; but when it is differentiated, [the following applies].
Otherwise, there would follow the consequence of perceiving the entity as before;
thus, even if one imagines that "it is concealed," one must state this alternative regarding the concealment itself— enough of this over-elaboration.
The refutation of the doctrine of momentariness according to the view of certain [opponents]:

Here, some explain it thus: “The single perceptual cognition designated as recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), which synthesizes ‘that-ness’ and ‘this-ness’ as mutually conjoined in the form ‘That very thing is this,’ sublates the inference of momentary destruction.”
And this is not correct:

these two cognitions, consisting of perception and recollection, being respectively occupied with the mere "that-ness" and the mere "this-ness," are not capable of manifesting the object as existing at the same time as the occurrence of the experience of both.
Because it contradicts experience;
for just as an object existing at the same place and time appears as a single unity, so too does an object existing at different places and times manifest as a single unity.
And since the arising of such an experience cannot occur without a single cognition,
this very cognition must be accepted as one.
To establish the existence of the effect, a cause— even if unperceived— must be postulated.
Furthermore, one should not investigate by looking toward the cause for a reversal of an effect that has been clearly perceived; for,

although this kind of cognition could not possibly arise from a sensory organ alone, nor from a mental impression (*saṃskāra*)— termed "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*)— which is produced solely from what was previously experienced.
Nevertheless, the teachers maintained that this effect arises from those two when they have attained a distinct state through their mutual conjunction.
Nor is this even appropriate:
that this [cognition] is not indeed perception,
even though there is the employment of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*).

Because its birth is dependent upon the operation of the sense faculties, it is no different from what is accepted as perception by all disputants at the time of its first occurrence, for which all disputes have been set aside. Furthermore, there is no evidence whatsoever that this is a fallacious means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*), since it is devoid of sublation, defects in the causes, or the awareness of another object.
Nor should one take pleasure in the thought that this very inference is the sublater [of the opponent's position],
because it would entail the fault of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*);
for as long as this cognition remains unsublated, [the inference cannot be established].
Therefore, inference itself is not even able to arise; and once an inference has arisen, this [opposing cognition] becomes sublated.
Furthermore, the condition for the arising of an inference is that its object must be unsublated.
Otherwise, why is coldness not inferred in fire?
[Objection: But in that case, how is the difference established through inference for flames and so forth, which are determined to be one?
[Response: This is an introduction of the dual nature of an entity according to the Bhaṭṭa school’s doctrine.
In this regard, they proclaim the essence of the established doctrine: all things consist of both the universal and the particular.
Among these, perception has the universal as its object, whereas inference has the particular as its object.

Since there is no contradiction between perception and inference when they operate within different domains, perception does not obstruct the arising of inference. But how, then, can that which is non-momentary possess causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritā*)?
They say "in succession.
Indeed, that entity, having acquired specific qualities through the conjunction of auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), brings about those various causal efficacies (*arthakriyā*) only in succession.
Now, is that which is conceptualized by the auxiliaries distinct [from the entity]?
Or, [the opponent might argue] that a particularity (viśeṣa) is imparted to that which is non-distinct; however, the refutations for this pair of alternatives have already been set forth previously.
Here too, they follow the same line of reasoning.
This is not our view that all things are exclusively distinct or exclusively non-distinct; rather,
we maintain that both difference and non-difference exist in all entities.

In this regard, the objections arising from the conceptualization of mere difference have been refuted by resorting to non-difference, and those based on mere non-difference by relying upon difference.
Now, one might ask: how can these two—difference and non-difference—reside together in a single locus, given that they are contradictory?
Regarding this, they say: these two are not contradictory, because they are observed together.
For contradiction is characterized by the impossibility of coexistence.
Furthermore, non-abiding is based on non-perception;
therefore, there is no contradiction. This is its refutation.
For he saw this: difference and non-difference cannot possibly exist in one and the same place, because they are contradictory. Indeed, their simultaneous perception is not possible;
for the very cognition of a single form is what constitutes the perception of non-difference.
The perception of distinct characteristics is the observation of difference. In that case, if there were a cognition of a single form,
then there would be no perception of distinct characteristics.
Furthermore, when distinct forms are perceived,
there is simply no perception of a single form;
therefore, it is not possible to establish causal efficiency by resorting to the distinction between difference and non-difference.
Nor does recognition contradict inference, because recognition itself is that which must be examined. An example is the cognition regarding mother-of-pearl: "This is that very same silver."
And since that [cognition] is based solely on the non-apprehension of difference due to similarity, an investigation is appropriate here as well.

When momentariness is determined through the investigation of the object by means of the impossibility of its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), it is then ascertained that "this is a deception caused by the successive arising of similar [moments]."
Furthermore, even for one who reflects, there occurs a reversal of a cognition that has arisen through the power of inference regarding such things as disorientation;
yet, in the case of fire and the like, the cognition of heat, though being examined, cannot be established otherwise,
and thus no inference of a reversal arises.
Therefore, enough of this persistent insistence on the view of deception;
this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Now, those who have seen the further shore of the ocean of the most profound and venerable teachings speak of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) regarding pillars and other such objects.

When things previously experienced are again perceived after having been interrupted by concealment or other causes, the cognition arises in one who experiences them once more: "This is that very same thing.
In this case, if purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) can somehow be accounted for even from a permanent entity, [then the cognition of identity would be justified].
Therefore, why should it be postulated that this conventional usage of non-difference is based on the non-apprehension of difference?

Furthermore, it is logically possible for even a stable entity to perform causal efficiency (arthakriyā) sequentially by means of specific qualities—such as adventitious action—arising through the power of auxiliary causes. And that specific quality is indeed distinct from the entity itself which performs the causal efficiency.
Nor is it logical that the entity which performs causal efficiency remains indifferent while that very same entity [is said to] act;
for its status as a means consists precisely in its being permeated by such a specific distinction.

The worldly convention regarding the status of things as "means" (sādhana) is based precisely on their connection with that specific quality by virtue of which an efficient action (arthakriyā) immediately follows.
But how, then, is this specific quality designated as "belonging to that"?
Because inference [establishes it] precisely by virtue of its being based on that.
But how is it that it is based on that?
It is because it arises through the power of its own cause; let this view be set aside.
Enough with our having followed you so far.
Now, why is it that the difference of the entity itself is not inferred?
We reply: because it would contradict recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).
And inference following what has been seen is appropriate, because it is a gateway for the occurrence of what has been seen;
just as purposeful action is seen in the case of what is perceived.
Likewise, this is also observed: that there is a stable entity (*sthāvara-bhāva*).
Therefore, an inference consistent with that is appropriate.

Consequently, since the pervasion of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) by either succession or simultaneity does not cease even in the case of a stable entity, the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) remains unestablished.
And since that [reason] is unestablished and there is no subverting argument (bādhaka) against its opposite,
existence is not capable of proving momentariness— which is invariably concomitant with that very [unestablished] state—
because it is inconclusive (anaikāntika).
Nor is existence merely the capacity for causal efficiency; rather, it is the fitness for connection with a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa),
because intrinsic existence itself consists in the fitness for connection with a means of valid cognition.
Even though it does not perform a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*),
there is nothing faulty in saying that it "exists"; as for what was stated— that entities are independent with respect to their destruction— [that too is untenable].
Even that, when scrutinized, dissolves like a lacquer ornament being consumed by fire.
What indeed do you gentlemen consider to be destruction?
If you say that destruction is non-existence through annihilation (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), then what, again, is this non-existence through annihilation?
If it were argued that cognitions such as "there is no milk in the curd" have existence as their object,
then the principle arising from the *amṛtakalā* must be extracted [as the correct response]:
for there is indeed no cognition that says "it does not exist."
However, when there is the experience of the very nature of curd itself as self-luminous, the use of the word "not" is merely verbal;
for that which is the non-existence of milk is precisely the perception of the very nature of curd even while that [milk] is visible.
Nor does milk alone possess causality with respect to that [curd] independently, since milk is observed even when another cause has not intervened.
Nor can it be said that this [milk] is not perceived as something other [than the curd],
because recognition establishes non-difference.
But surely, if there were dependence on another cause, its necessary occurrence (dhruvabhāvitā) would not be possible?
The state of being invariably produced is not tenable. How is it known that it is indeed invariably produced?
If you say, "Because it is observed"?
"One must necessarily exist by means of another cause"—
let this be understood simply from what has been shown.
Nor are we fools, such that we would be intimidated by such talk.
Furthermore, as for this [objection]: even though things that are perishable arise from their own causes,
if their destruction were dependent on another cause,
then it would follow— just as before— that the thing would still be perceived and so forth, even after a distinct [destruction] had arisen.
To this it is replied: We have already stated that the very perception of the subtle element (*tanmātra*) is its destruction.
Therefore, because the cause for that [destruction] exists, it must occur by means of that [perception] itself.
Furthermore, non-perception of it is also that same [perception]; thus, non-perception itself is not the perception of it.

And since the conventional usage of "non-existence" is also based upon that [momentary destruction], everything is free from confusion. This protection of the life-force, consisting of the vital points, has been prescribed in the Mīmāṃsā for those whose vitals have been licked by the fire-poison of the venomous snake of momentary flux belonging to the Sugata. // 1 //
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Protection of the Life of Mīmāṃsā," in the *Prakaraṇapañcikā* composed by the Great Professor Śrī Śālikanātha Miśra.
